title: 2 Samuel 12:16–25
context: The child becomes ill. David fasts and pleads with God for seven days, lying on the ground. When the child dies, his servants fear to tell him, but David perceives it, rises, washes, worships in the LORD’s house and eats. He explains that while the child lived he hoped the LORD might be gracious, but now he cannot bring him back: he will go to him, but the child will not return. Then David comforts Bathsheba, and Solomon is born. The LORD loves the child and sends Nathan to name him Jedidiah. This is a passage of grief, and it calls for gentleness. Interpreters within both traditions differ on what David’s words in verse 23 imply and on the destiny of infants who die. Both traditions see Solomon’s birth as grace after judgment.

verses.text: David therefore begged God for the child; and David fasted, and went in and lay all night on the ground.
verses.arminianNotes:
David pleads with God for the child, fasts, and lies all night on the ground. He intercedes earnestly.

Arminian readers note that David’s prayer shows his belief that God’s announced judgments may sometimes be turned by repentance and prayer, as with Nineveh (Jonah 3:10), and that pleading with God is a fitting response to grief.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s intercession, even after the prophetic word, shows that prayer is a right response to God’s dealings, and that God ordains prayer as a means of seeking his mercy even when the outcome is in his hands.

Both traditions honor David’s earnest prayer and humble fasting.

verses.text: The elders of his house arose beside him, to raise him up from the earth; but he would not, and he didn’t eat bread with them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The elders of his household try to raise him from the ground, but he refuses and will not eat with them. David’s grief is intense.

Arminian readers note that the household’s concern shows the depth of David’s distress, and that grief and repentance can be inseparable when sin has brought suffering on someone loved.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s refusal to be comforted reflects the seriousness with which he now takes his sin and its consequences, a sign of the godly sorrow that leads to repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10).

Both traditions read David’s grief with compassion and see in it the reality of his repentance.

verses.text: On the seventh day, the child died. David’s servants were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, “Behold, while the child was yet alive, we spoke to him and he didn’t listen to our voice. How will he then harm himself if we tell him that the child is dead?”
verses.arminianNotes:
On the seventh day the child dies, and David’s servants fear to tell him, wondering what harm he might do himself if he would not listen to them while the child lived. They fear for his well-being.

Arminian readers note that the servants’ fear shows how deeply grief had gripped David, and that the narrative treats the child’s death as a real loss, not a mere lesson.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the child’s death comes as Nathan had said, showing that God’s word is sure, and that the servants’ concern reflects the community’s care for a grieving king.

Both traditions mourn the child and read the verse with gentleness, as a moment of grief in David’s household.

verses.text: But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, David perceived that the child was dead; and David said to his servants, “Is the child dead?” They said, “He is dead.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Seeing his servants whispering, David realizes the child is dead and asks, and they tell him he is dead. The news is confirmed.

Arminian readers note that David perceives the truth before he is told, and that the simple exchange conveys the weight of loss without embellishment, inviting readers to sit with grief.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the quiet, restrained narration gives the moment dignity, and that the confirmation of the child’s death sets up David’s surprising response, which reveals his understanding of God.

Both traditions read the verse as a moment of profound sorrow that calls for compassion rather than analysis.

verses.text: Then David arose from the earth, and washed and anointed himself, and changed his clothing; and he came into the LORD’s house, and worshiped. Then he came to his own house; and when he requested, they set bread before him and he ate.
verses.arminianNotes:
David rises, washes, anoints himself, changes clothes, goes into the LORD’s house and worships, then goes home and eats. David worships in grief.

Arminian readers note that David’s turning to worship shows a heart that has accepted God’s judgment and still trusts in God’s goodness, a model of faith in sorrow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s worship after the child’s death expresses submission to God’s sovereign will, similar to Job’s worship in loss (Job 1:20–21), and that true faith can bless God even through tears. The LORD’s house here would be the tent for the ark (6:17).

Both traditions see David’s worship as a profound act of faith in grief.

verses.text: Then his servants said to him, “What is this that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive, but when the child was dead, you rose up and ate bread.”
verses.arminianNotes:
His servants ask why he fasted and wept while the child lived but now rises and eats. His behavior puzzles them.

Arminian readers note that David’s servants expected grief after death, not before, and their question opens the way for David to explain how his faith shaped both his pleading and his acceptance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the servants’ question highlights how David’s conduct was shaped by his understanding of God rather than by convention, and prepares for his answer about hope and acceptance.

Both traditions see the question as inviting reflection on how believers grieve, and both read David’s change as rooted in faith rather than indifference.

verses.text: He said, “While the child was yet alive, I fasted and wept; for I said, ‘Who knows whether the LORD will not be gracious to me, that the child may live?’
verses.arminianNotes:
David says that while the child lived he fasted and wept, thinking the LORD might be gracious and let the child live. He hoped in God’s mercy.

Arminian readers note that David’s words show that he thought God’s announced judgment might be relented from, and that prayer engages a God who responds to his people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s hope rested on God’s gracious character, and that his prayer was not an attempt to force God’s hand but an appeal to his mercy, made in humility before God’s sovereign will.

Both traditions agree that David rightly prayed, and both affirm that God hears the prayers of his people, though they explain the relation between prayer and God’s purposes differently.

verses.text: But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David says that now the child is dead there is no point in fasting; he cannot bring him back; he will go to him, but the child will not return to him. David accepts the loss.

Arminian readers note that some interpreters take David’s words as hope of reunion beyond death, while others take them to mean he too will go to the grave; views differ within the tradition, and comfort for grieving parents rests finally on God’s goodness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the same range of readings appears among Reformed interpreters, as do differing views on infants who die, and many in both traditions find in this verse a quiet hope; the text does not settle the question.

Both traditions treat the verse with pastoral gentleness and trust the child to the mercy of God.

verses.text: David comforted Bathsheba his wife, and went in to her, and lay with her. She bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. The LORD loved him;
verses.arminianNotes:
David comforts Bathsheba his wife, and she bears a son whom he names Solomon, and the LORD loves him. She is now called his wife.

Arminian readers note that the narrator now names her as David’s wife and shows David comforting her in shared grief, and that God’s love for Solomon shows grace extended after judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s love for Solomon is a sovereign and gracious choice, and that the son through whom the Davidic line will continue (7:12–13) comes from this marriage, showing grace triumphing over sin without excusing it. The name Solomon is commonly connected with the Hebrew word for peace.

Both traditions see Solomon’s birth as grace after judgment.

verses.text: and he sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, and he named him Jedidiah, for the LORD’s sake.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD sends word through Nathan the prophet and names the child Jedidiah, for the LORD’s sake. The name means loved by the LORD.

Arminian readers note that the same prophet who brought rebuke now brings a word of love, showing that God’s purpose in rebuke is restoration, and that God’s favor is extended anew to David’s house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the name Jedidiah, given by God himself, declares divine favor that rests on grace rather than merit, and that God’s covenant purposes for David’s line continue despite David’s sin.

Both traditions read the naming as a tender assurance of God’s love and see Nathan’s two visits as rebuke and grace held together.
